claim: Bath application of 100 nM IVM to acute brain slices suppressed neuronal firing by up to 90% in YFP+ entorhinal neurons from GlyCl transgenic mice.
source: Bath application of 100 nM IVM to acute brain slices suppressed neuronal firing by up to 90% in YFP+ entorhinal neurons from GlyCl transgenic mice, but had no effect on EC neurons from control animals (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: IVM had no effect on EC neurons from control animals.
source: Bath application of 100 nM IVM to acute brain slices suppressed neuronal firing by up to 90% in YFP+ entorhinal neurons from GlyCl transgenic mice, but had no effect on EC neurons from control animals (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: The drug half-life of IVM is >12 hr.
source: We previously demonstrated that systemic administration of IVM decreased neuronal firing in vivo for several hours after intraperitoneal injection and that the drug half-life of >12 hr likely maintained this effect for a day or more (Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Systemic administration of IVM decreased neuronal firing in vivo for several hours after intraperitoneal injection.
source: We previously demonstrated that systemic administration of IVM decreased neuronal firing in vivo for several hours after intraperitoneal injection and that the drug half-life of >12 hr likely maintained this effect for a day or more (Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Animals injected with a single dose of IVM (5 mg/kg, i.p.) showed diminished DG axonal labeling within 1–2 days post injection.
source: In contrast, animals injected with a single dose of IVM (5 mg/kg, i.p.) showed diminished DG axonal labeling within 1–2 days post injection (dpi) and labeling was nearly undetectable by 4 dpi.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DG axonal labeling was nearly undetectable by 4 dpi after IVM injection.
source: In contrast, animals injected with a single dose of IVM (5 mg/kg, i.p.) showed diminished DG axonal labeling within 1–2 days post injection (dpi) and labeling was nearly undetectable by 4 dpi.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The number of labeled cell bodies in EC2 was significantly decreased by 4 dpi after IVM injection.
source: Alongside this change in the DG, the number of labeled cell bodies in EC2 was significantly decreased by 4 dpi and reduced by 50% at 7 dpi (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The number of labeled cell bodies in EC2 was reduced by 50% at 7 dpi after IVM injection.
source: Alongside this change in the DG, the number of labeled cell bodies in EC2 was significantly decreased by 4 dpi and reduced by 50% at 7 dpi (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Many YFP-labeled EC2 axons had withdrawn from the DG into the cortex and developed pronounced swellings at their distal ends.
source: First, we saw that many YFP-labeled EC2 axons had withdrawn from the DG into the cortex and developed pronounced swellings at their distal ends.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining images shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The swellings at the distal ends of EC2 axons were strongly reminiscent of retraction bulbs, which are typically observed after axonal injury or physical lesion.
source: These swellings were strongly reminiscent of retraction bulbs, which are typically observed after axonal injury or physical lesion (Hill et al., 2016; Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to known phenomena in the literature and images in Figure 1C.

claim: Retraction bulbs appeared within 1 day of IVM treatment.
source: These bulbs appeared within 1 day of IVM treatment, peaked at 2–3 dpi, and were gone over the same time course as the loss of YFP-labeled cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Retraction bulbs peaked at 2–3 dpi after IVM treatment.
source: These bulbs appeared within 1 day of IVM treatment, peaked at 2–3 dpi, and were gone over the same time course as the loss of YFP-labeled cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: EC2 cells were labeled with active caspase-3 in the days immediately following IVM injection.
source: Next, we found EC2 cells labeled with active caspase-3, indicative of apoptotic cell death, in the days immediately following IVM injection (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Active caspase-3 labeling is indicative of apoptotic cell death.
source: Next, we found EC2 cells labeled with active caspase-3, indicative of apoptotic cell death, in the days immediately following IVM injection (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about caspase-3 function.

claim: Caspase-labeled cells were sporadic, but only observed in EC2 of animals subjected to entorhinal silencing.
source: Caspase-labeled cells were sporadic, but only observed in EC2 of animals subjected to entorhinal silencing.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining observations.

claim: EC2 cells contained a caspase-cleaved actin fragment (fractin), suggesting apoptotic cell death.
source: Consistent with caspase activation, we observed that EC2 cells contained a caspase-cleaved actin fragment (fractin), again suggesting apoptotic cell death (Schulz et al., 2009; Yang et al., 1998; Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D and citations to literature.

claim: Fractin labeling was robust and peaked between 4 and 7 days after IVM.
source: Fractin labeling was robust, peaked between 4 and 7 days after IVM and then abated, presumably after the dead and dying cells had been cleared.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Hypertrophic Iba1+ microglia were observed in both the DG and the EC after IVM treatment.
source: Finally, we observed hypertrophic Iba1+ microglia in both the DG and the EC.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Iba1 staining increased by 2 days after IVM.
source: Iba1 staining increased by 2 days after IVM, peaked by 4–7 dpi, and receded by 10–13 dpi (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Iba1 staining peaked by 4–7 dpi after IVM.
source: Iba1 staining increased by 2 days after IVM, peaked by 4–7 dpi, and receded by 10–13 dpi (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Iba1 staining receded by 10–13 dpi after IVM.
source: Iba1 staining increased by 2 days after IVM, peaked by 4–7 dpi, and receded by 10–13 dpi (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Transient neuronal silencing of EC2 neurons initiated a cascade of events beginning with axonal retraction and ending in caspase-associated cell death with a strong but focal microglial response.
source: Collectively, our data suggests that transient neuronal silencing of EC2 neurons initiated a cascade of events beginning with axonal retraction and ending in caspase-associated cell death with a strong but focal microglial response.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference from multiple experimental observations.

claim: EC2 cells were diminished in animals carrying both lacZ and GlyCl after IVM treatment.
source: We again found that EC2 cells were diminished in animals carrying both lacZ and GlyCl but detected no cell loss in mice expressing lacZ alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: No cell loss was detected in mice expressing lacZ alone after IVM treatment.
source: We again found that EC2 cells were diminished in animals carrying both lacZ and GlyCl but detected no cell loss in mice expressing lacZ alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: GlyCl-based neuronal silencing and not IVM exposure alone was responsible for cell death in the Nop-GlyCl mice.
source: This data demonstrates that GlyCl-based neuronal silencing and not IVM exposure alone was responsible for cell death in the Nop-GlyCl mice.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the comparison of GlyCl+lacZ and lacZ-only mice.

claim: Viral expression of Kir2.1 peaked at approximately 7 dpi.
source: Viral expression peaked at approximately 7 dpi, when field recordings of input–output responses in the perforant path demonstrated a significant reduction in transmission between EC2 and DG (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Field recordings of input–output responses in the perforant path demonstrated a significant reduction in transmission between EC2 and DG at 7 dpi after Kir2.1 viral injection.
source: Viral expression peaked at approximately 7 dpi, when field recordings of input–output responses in the perforant path demonstrated a significant reduction in transmission between EC2 and DG (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Loss of axonal labeling from the DG over the following weeks after Kir2.1 expression was qualitatively similar to, but slower than, what was observed with GlyCl silencing.
source: Co-expressed YFP again allowed us to visualize the loss of axonal labeling from the DG over the following weeks that was qualitatively similar to, but slower than, what we observed with GlyCl silencing (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of imaging data between Kir2.1 and GlyCl experiments.

claim: Retraction bulbs were not seen in the EC of Kir2.1 mice.
source: Unlike the GlyCl model, we did not see retraction bulbs in the EC of Kir2.1 mice, but did observe evidence of axon damage in the DG at later time points.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging observations.

claim: Evidence of axon damage in the DG was observed at later time points in Kir2.1 mice.
source: Unlike the GlyCl model, we did not see retraction bulbs in the EC of Kir2.1 mice, but did observe evidence of axon damage in the DG at later time points.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging observations.

claim: Iba1 immunostaining peaked between 13 and 16 dpi in both EC and DG of Kir-expressing animals.
source: Iba1 immunostaining peaked between 13 and 16 dpi in both EC and DG of Kir-expressing animals, consistent with neuronal damage in these areas (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,F.

claim: GlyCl expression was sufficient to suppress neuronal firing in pre- and parasubiculum upon bath application of 100 nM IVM.
source: We first confirmed that GlyCl expression was sufficient to suppress neuronal firing in pre- and parasubiculum using whole-cell recordings in acute brain slices. Action potential firing was significantly reduced in YFP+ neurons in both regions upon bath application of 100 nM IVM to the same level as EC2 at this dose (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Action potential firing was significantly reduced in YFP+ neurons in both pre- and parasubiculum upon bath application of 100 nM IVM to the same level as EC2 at this dose.
source: We first confirmed that GlyCl expression was sufficient to suppress neuronal firing in pre- and parasubiculum using whole-cell recordings in acute brain slices. Action potential firing was significantly reduced in YFP+ neurons in both regions upon bath application of 100 nM IVM to the same level as EC2 at this dose (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: A single dose of IVM (5 mg/kg) significantly reduced the number of labeled EC2 cells in GlyCl+ mice.
source: As before, a single dose of IVM significantly reduced the number of labeled EC2 cells in GlyCl+ mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: IVM (5 mg/kg) caused no loss of pre- or parasubiculum neurons.
source: In contrast, IVM caused no loss of pre- or parasubiculum neurons at this dose, suggesting that these neighboring regions may not share EC2's vulnerability to activity disruption (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A dose of 10 mg/kg IVM (2× IVM) caused significantly more cell loss in the EC2 than 5 mg/kg IVM (1× IVM) (70% at 2× vs. 50% at 1×).
source: This dose caused significantly more cell loss in the EC2 than 1× IVM (70% at 2× vs. 50% at 1×, Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Parasubiculum neurons that had been resistant to 1× IVM showed mild cell loss at 2× IVM.
source: We also found that parasubiculum neurons that had been resistant to 1× IVM now showed mild cell loss at 2× IVM (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The proportion of neurons lost in parasubiculum at 2× IVM (30%) was considerably smaller than in EC2 at 1× IVM (50%).
source: Nevertheless, the proportion of neurons lost in parasubiculum at 2× IVM (30%) was considerably smaller than in EC2 at 1× IVM (50%).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of cell count data.

claim: Neuron counts in presubiculum were not altered at either dose of IVM.
source: Remarkably, neuron counts in presubiculum were not altered at either dose.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The presubiculum expressed relatively low levels of GlyCl receptor.
source: We found that the presubiculum expressed relatively low levels of GlyCl receptor, and therefore we could not exclude the possibility that its resilience was a result of low transgene expression (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: GlyCl expression was practically identical in EC2 and parasubiculum.
source: In contrast, GlyCl expression was practically identical in EC2 and parasubiculum, despite their distinct patterns of cell loss (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: EC2 neurons are especially sensitive to activity perturbation, and considerably more vulnerable to electrical inactivation than cells in neighboring pre- and parasubiculum.
source: These findings suggest that EC2 neurons are especially sensitive to activity perturbation, and considerably more vulnerable to electrical inactivation than cells in neighboring pre- and parasubiculum.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the differential vulnerability data across brain regions.

claim: The Nop-tTA driver line is active in both reelin-positive stellate cells and Wfs1-positive pyramidal neurons.
source: We found that the Nop-tTA driver line is active in both reelin-positive stellate cells and Wfs1-positive pyramidal neurons, but completely absent from inhibitory neurons (Figure 3A and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The Nop-tTA driver line is completely absent from inhibitory neurons.
source: We found that the Nop-tTA driver line is active in both reelin-positive stellate cells and Wfs1-positive pyramidal neurons, but completely absent from inhibitory neurons (Figure 3A and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining observations.

claim: YFP labeled roughly half of the reelin- and Wfs1-expressing EC2 neurons.
source: Consistent with past work, we found YFP labeled roughly half of the reelin- and Wfs1-expressing EC2 neurons (Yasuda and Mayford, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining observations and citation to previous work.

claim: Only reelin-expressing cells decreased after IVM, while the number of Wfs1-positive cells did not change significantly.
source: Of the two cell types, only reelin-expressing cells decreased after IVM, while the number of Wfs1-positive cells did not change significantly (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Reelin + stellate cells are preferentially vulnerable to cell death after silencing.
source: This data suggests that reelin + stellate cells are preferentially vulnerable to cell death after silencing.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the differential cell loss data between reelin+ and Wfs1+ cells.

claim: The parasubiculum is comprised predominantly of Wfs1+ cells.
source: This conclusion coincides with the fact that the parasubiculum, comprised predominantly of Wfs1+ cells, was resistant to neuronal silencing (Figures 2E and 3D), and with recent work suggesting that expression of Wfs1 is protective in the EC during AD (Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Expression of Wfs1 is protective in the EC during AD.
source: This conclusion coincides with the fact that the parasubiculum, comprised predominantly of Wfs1+ cells, was resistant to neuronal silencing (Figures 2E and 3D), and with recent work suggesting that expression of Wfs1 is protective in the EC during AD (Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: TeTX expression significantly reduced electrical transmission between EC2 and DG.
source: Field recording in acute slices from virally injected mice confirmed that TeTX expression significantly reduced electrical transmission between EC2 and DG and that the extent of suppression was consistent with the percentage of neurons expressing the virus (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The extent of suppression by TeTX was consistent with the percentage of neurons expressing the virus.
source: Field recording in acute slices from virally injected mice confirmed that TeTX expression significantly reduced electrical transmission between EC2 and DG and that the extent of suppression was consistent with the percentage of neurons expressing the virus (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: YFP intensity began to fade in the DG of TeTX mice shortly after viral expression peaked at 7 dpi.
source: Viral expression peaked at 7 dpi and shortly afterward YFP intensity began to fade in the DG of TeTX mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Loss of perforant path labeling in TeTX mice progressed over the next 2 weeks until nearly undetectable.
source: Loss of perforant path labeling progressed over the next 2 weeks until nearly undetectable.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Animals injected with YFP alone showed no change in labeling over the same time period as TeTX mice.
source: Animals injected with YFP alone showed no change in labeling over the same time period.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Loss of axonal labeling in TeTX mice was accompanied by the emergence of fractin staining in the EC that was specific to mice expressing TeTX.
source: Loss of axonal labeling in TeTX mice was accompanied by the emergence of fractin staining in the EC that was specific to mice expressing TeTX (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Fractin-positive cells first appeared at 10 dpi in TeTX mice.
source: Fractin-positive cells first appeared at 10 dpi, became more prominent at 13 dpi, and largely abated by 19 dpi.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Fractin-positive cells became more prominent at 13 dpi in TeTX mice.
source: Fractin-positive cells first appeared at 10 dpi, became more prominent at 13 dpi, and largely abated by 19 dpi.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Fractin-positive cells largely abated by 19 dpi in TeTX mice.
source: Fractin-positive cells first appeared at 10 dpi, became more prominent at 13 dpi, and largely abated by 19 dpi.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Reactive microglia were observed in the DG and EC as an early marker of impending cell loss in TeTX mice.
source: As with GlyCl-based silencing, we observed reactive microglia in the DG and EC as an early marker of impending cell loss (Figure 4E) and found sporadic cells labeled with active caspase 3 (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Sporadic cells labeled with active caspase 3 were found in TeTX mice.
source: As with GlyCl-based silencing, we observed reactive microglia in the DG and EC as an early marker of impending cell loss (Figure 4E) and found sporadic cells labeled with active caspase 3 (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Inhibiting synaptic release alone is sufficient to cause EC2 cell loss.
source: This cascade of events leading from impaired neurotransmission to cell death was comparable across the various silencing methods we tested, suggesting that EC2 neurons are broadly susceptible to inactivity, and that inhibiting synaptic release alone is sufficient to cause EC2 cell loss.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the TeTX experiments showing cell loss without electrical silencing.

claim: GlyCl silencing was characterized by the appearance of retraction bulbs in deep layers of EC.
source: Although electrical suppression by GlyCl caused gradual loss of DG fluorescence, synaptic inhibition by TeTX caused pronounced axonal disintegration within the DG (Figure 5). GlyCl silencing was characterized by the appearance of retraction bulbs in deep layers of EC, suggesting neuronal loss followed intact axonal withdraw.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: No retraction bulbs were visible in TeTX-treated animals.
source: No retraction bulbs were visible in TeTX-treated animals; instead, the axonal processes became fragmented with small bright puncta that were reminiscent of Wallerian degeneration.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The axonal processes in TeTX-treated animals became fragmented with small bright puncta that were reminiscent of Wallerian degeneration.
source: No retraction bulbs were visible in TeTX-treated animals; instead, the axonal processes became fragmented with small bright puncta that were reminiscent of Wallerian degeneration.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5 and comparison to known phenomena.

claim: The Nop-tTA driver line is active in approximately 40% of EC2 neurons.
source: The Nop-tTA driver line used to express GlyCl, Kir2.1, and TeTX is active in approximately 40% of EC2 neurons (Yasuda and Mayford, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: During postnatal development, competition between active and inactive neurons is used to refine the perforant path.
source: During postnatal development, competition between active and inactive neurons is used to refine the perforant path (Yasuda et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: TeTX silencing of the same neuronal subset caused axonal loss in the developing brain that was qualitatively similar to what was seen in the adult.
source: TeTX silencing of the same neuronal subset caused axonal loss in the developing brain that was qualitatively similar to what we saw in the adult.
evidence: The claim is an inference from comparison to developmental studies.

claim: Yasuda et al. showed that axonal loss could be prevented by eliminating the competition between active and inactive cells with tetrodotoxin (TTX).
source: Yasuda et al. further showed that axonal loss could be prevented by eliminating the competition between active and inactive cells with tetrodotoxin (TTX).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: TTX infusion preserved axonal innervation in mice expressing TeTX.
source: In contrast, axonal labeling remained robust and intact in mice infused with TTX.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Preservation of axonal innervation by TTX was limited to the infused hemisphere.
source: Preservation of axonal innervation was limited to the infused hemisphere; degeneration on the contralateral side was identical to that seen in animals infused with saline (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The extent of microglial activation normally observed in the DG of TeTX mice was abated by TTX infusion.
source: Consistent with the axon preservation, the extent of microglial activation normally observed in the DG of TeTX mice was also abated by TTX infusion (Figure 6B and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6B and E.

claim: TTX infusion preserved axonal innervation and maintained microglial homeostasis in mice expressing TeTX, suggesting that degeneration due to synaptic silencing may be governed by ongoing competition between active and inactive contacts.
source: In conclusion, TTX infusion preserved axonal innervation and maintained microglial homeostasis in mice expressing TeTX, suggesting that degeneration due to synaptic silencing may be governed by ongoing competition between active and inactive contacts.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the TTX rescue experiments.

claim: Infusion of TTX had no effect on neuronal survival in the GlyCl model.
source: Contrary to our results with TeTX, infusion of TTX had no effect on neuronal survival in the GlyCl model.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: TTX infusion had no effect on fractin expression or microglial activation evoked by IVM in the GlyCl model.
source: TTX infusion also had no effect on fractin expression or microglial activation evoked by IVM (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: TTX infusion by itself does not cause cell loss.
source: Importantly, TTX infusion caused no cell loss in control mice injected with vehicle instead of IVM, indicating that TTX infusion by itself does not cause cell death.
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cell death in the GlyCl model cannot be explained by competition between the silenced cells and their active neighbors.
source: These findings indicate that cell death in the GlyCl model cannot be explained by competition between the silenced cells and their active neighbors, and that separate mechanisms govern neuronal death following electrical versus synaptic silencing.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the differential effects of TTX on TeTX vs. GlyCl models.

claim: Separate mechanisms govern neuronal death following electrical versus synaptic silencing.
source: These findings indicate that cell death in the GlyCl model cannot be explained by competition between the silenced cells and their active neighbors, and that separate mechanisms govern neuronal death following electrical versus synaptic silencing.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the differential effects of TTX on TeTX vs. GlyCl models.

claim: Mature EC2 neurons require ongoing activity for survival long beyond the postnatal critical period.
source: First, we demonstrate that mature EC2 neurons require ongoing activity for survival long beyond the postnatal critical period.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings from the silencing experiments.

claim: This activity dependence distinguishes EC from neighboring pre- and parasubiculum, which are largely resilient to activity changes.
source: This activity dependence distinguishes EC from neighboring pre- and parasubiculum, which are largely resilient to activity changes.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the differential vulnerability findings.

claim: Electrical versus synaptic silencing can elicit distinct forms of axonal damage prior to cell death.
source: Second, we demonstrate that electrical versus synaptic silencing can elicit distinct forms of axonal damage prior to cell death.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the findings comparing GlyCl and TeTX phenotypes.

claim: Axonal disintegration due to synaptic silencing is governed by competition between active and inactive neurons.
source: Finally, we show that axonal disintegration due to synaptic silencing is governed by competition between active and inactive neurons, suggesting that this circuit may maintain an activity-dependent critical period well into adulthood.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the TTX rescue findings.

claim: Both electrical silencing due to chloride or potassium flux and synaptic silencing due to arrest of neurotransmitter release are each sufficient to cause axonal damage of EC2 neurons followed by cell body demise.
source: We show that both electrical silencing due to chloride or potassium flux and synaptic silencing due to arrest of neurotransmitter release are each sufficient to cause axonal damage of EC2 neurons followed by cell body demise.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the findings across different silencing methods.

claim: Wholesale changes in activity-dependent circuit patterning are traditionally thought to be limited to a brief window during postnatal development.
source: Such wholesale changes in activity-dependent circuit patterning are traditionally thought to be limited to a brief window during postnatal development (Murase, 2014; Wong and Marín, 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: Numerous studies have used chemical, chemogenetic, or optogenetic tools to silence entorhinal input to the DG without observing signs of axonal damage or cell death.
source: Numerous studies have used chemical, chemogenetic, or optogenetic tools to silence entorhinal input to the DG without observing signs of axonal damage or cell death (Rueckemann et al., 2016; Miao et al., 2015; Ormond and McNaughton, 2015; Rowland et al., 2018; Robinson et al., 2017; Kanter et al., 2017; van Wijngaarden et al., 2020; Heys et al., 2020; Qin et al., 2018; Rodriguez et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: The half-life for IVM in the brain is over 13 hr.
source: The half-life for IVM in the brain is over 13 hr and behavioral impairments persist for several days after IVM administration (Zhao et al., 2016; Lerchner et al., 2007 and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Behavioral impairments persist for several days after IVM administration.
source: The half-life for IVM in the brain is over 13 hr and behavioral impairments persist for several days after IVM administration (Zhao et al., 2016; Lerchner et al., 2007 and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work and unpublished data.

claim: Pyramidal neurons were relatively resilient to activity perturbation, while stellate cells were preferentially vulnerable.
source: Of the two populations, we found that pyramidal neurons were relatively resilient to activity perturbation, while stellate cells were preferentially vulnerable.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the differential vulnerability findings between cell types.

claim: Wfs1 expression protects EC2 neurons from tauopathy and degeneration.
source: This outcome is consistent with recent work showing that Wfs1 expression protects EC2 neurons from tauopathy and degeneration (Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: Tau tangles appear in dense patches within human EC2.
source: Tau tangles appear in dense patches within human EC2 (Braak and Braak, 1995; Van Hoesen et al., 1986; Van Hoesen et al., 1991), where, in contrast to the mouse EC, islands are composed of reelin+ stellate cells (Witter et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In human EC2, islands are composed of reelin+ stellate cells, in contrast to the mouse EC.
source: Tau tangles appear in dense patches within human EC2 (Braak and Braak, 1995; Van Hoesen et al., 1986; Van Hoesen et al., 1991), where, in contrast to the mouse EC, islands are composed of reelin+ stellate cells (Witter et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Both Wfs1+ and reelin+ cells are lost from EC2 during AD.
source: Both Wfs1+ and reelin+ cells are lost from EC2 during AD; however, the loss of reelin appears to be much more profound while more than half of Wfs1+ cells survive late into the disease (Chen et al., 2022; Chin et al., 2007; Delpech et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The loss of reelin appears to be much more profound than Wfs1+ cells during AD, while more than half of Wfs1+ cells survive late into the disease.
source: Both Wfs1+ and reelin+ cells are lost from EC2 during AD; however, the loss of reelin appears to be much more profound while more than half of Wfs1+ cells survive late into the disease (Chen et al., 2022; Chin et al., 2007; Delpech et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Synaptic markers are lost early in AD from the terminal field of EC2 neurons in DG.
source: Synaptic markers are also lost early in AD from the terminal field of EC2 neurons in DG, lending further support to the preferential vulnerability of hippocampal-projecting stellate and fan cells (Hamos et al., 1989; Scheff et al., 1996; Scheff et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Axons silenced by GlyCl displayed evidence of simple axonal retraction beginning within 1–2 days of silencing onset.
source: Axons silenced by GlyCl displayed evidence of simple axonal retraction beginning within 1–2 days of silencing onset.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Atrophy in TeTX-expressing axons was reminiscent of Wallerian degeneration, which is characterized by axon blebbing and fragmentation.
source: Atrophy in TeTX-expressing axons was reminiscent of Wallerian degeneration, which is characterized by axon blebbing and fragmentation.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data and comparison to known phenomena.
